analysis.one_liner: Lets victims of AI sexual deepfakes and leaked intimate images sue their creators and spreaders for damages.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill without a single objection on January 13, 2026, and it has sat at the House desk without a vote since the same day.
analysis.plain_summary: The DEFIANCE Act creates a new federal lawsuit that victims of sexually explicit AI 'deepfakes' and nonconsensually shared intimate photos can file against the people who make, share, or request that material. Victims could recover set damages of $150,000 (or $250,000 when the abuse is connected to sexual assault, stalking, or harassment), the offender's profits, punitive damages, court orders to delete the images, and attorney fees. Victims get 10 years to sue, with the clock starting when they discover the violation or turn 18, whichever is later.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of image-based sexual abuse, who are disproportionately women and minors. The bill's own findings describe victims suffering harassment, extortion, depression, and withdrawal from public life, often without ever learning who made the fake. The new federal lawsuit gives them a way to win money, force removal of the images, and keep their names out of public court filings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of sexual deepfakes and leaked images

how_it_helps.text: Creates a first-ever federal civil action allowing an identifiable person to sue anyone who knowingly produces, shares, or solicits and receives an intimate AI-generated forgery of them without consent.

Expands damages in existing nonconsensual-image lawsuits to include punitive damages and the offender's profits from the conduct, plus set damages of $150,000, rising to $250,000 when tied to sexual assault, stalking, or harassment.
Allows courts to order defendants to delete or stop displaying the images, and to shield victims with pseudonyms, redacted filings, and protective orders.
Gives victims 10 years to sue, with the clock starting only when they discover the violation or turn 18, whichever is later.
Lets states and tribal governments adopt even stronger protections without being preempted.

analysis.who_pays: People who knowingly create, share, or request nonconsensual intimate imagery, who would owe substantial damages and the victim's legal fees; platforms and site operators that disclose such content would also face suit. The cost is deliberately structured to fall on the offenders and profiteers, not taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Creators and spreaders of nonconsensual intimate imagery

drawbacks.text: Set damages of $150,000 to $250,000 per violation can be awarded without proof of actual financial loss, which imposes very large sums on individual defendants regardless of their means.

Civil liability for producing, or even possessing with intent to share, realistic AI depictions of real people raises free-speech questions about how far courts and Congress can go in regulating computer-generated images, a concern civil liberties groups have raised with similar legislation.

Enforcement is often impractical: the bill's own findings note that victims frequently cannot determine who created the content, so lawsuits will often reach only the people who shared or hosted the images rather than the original creator.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a documented, serious harm with a remedy aimed at offenders rather than at the technology itself, since liability requires knowledge of non-consent or intent to disclose. The honest objections are the speech-law tension in penalizing realistic synthetic images and the reality that many victims will never be able to identify the creator to sue. On balance, the targeted design keeps the overreach risk modest relative to the harm it remedies.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it without objection on January 13, 2026, and the House has held it at the desk ever since without scheduling a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 21, 2025, and referred to the Judiciary Committee.
On January 13, 2026, the Senate Judiciary Committee discharged the bill and the Senate passed it without amendment by unanimous consent.
The bill was sent to the House the same day and held at the desk, with no further action taken since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Victims gained a unanimous Senate endorsement of a federal remedy, but because the bill has not become law, operators and creators of nonconsensual intimate imagery continue to face no additional federal civil liability under it. The people who benefit most from the current state of affairs are those the bill would have made liable.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Deepfake operators and platforms, for now

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on May 21, 2025.

against.name: Speaker Mike Johnson
against.what_they_did: The House received the bill on January 13, 2026, held it at the desk, and has scheduled no vote or other action since.

against.name: Civil liberties groups (e.g., ACLU, EFF)
against.what_they_did: Publicly raised First Amendment concerns about civil liability for AI-generated intimate imagery of real people in connection with similar deepfake legislation.

sides.party_line_note: The Senate passed it by unanimous consent with no recorded opposition, and its eight cosponsors split four Democrats, three Republicans, and one Independent.

industries.note: The bill exposes anyone who knowingly produces an intimate forgery with intent to disclose it, or who knows the subject did not consent and would be harmed, to federal damages suits. App providers profiting from tools used for image-based sexual abuse would face direct financial risk they do not face today.

Platforms and site operators that disclose, or solicit and receive, nonconsensual intimate forgeries can be sued for the victim's set damages, the offender's profits, and punitive damages. The bill does not target lawful hosting generally, but it removes the current free pass for hosting this material.

Developers face liability only for knowingly producing a forgery with intent to disclose or with knowledge of the victim's non-consent and likely harm, so general-purpose AI tools are largely untouched. The broader AI industry keeps its market while bad actors lose legal cover.

analysis.trajectory: The House has taken no action since the bill arrived at the desk in January 2026. Senate-passed bills held at the desk often die without a House vote unless leadership schedules floor time or the measure is folded into a larger package; the unanimous Senate support and bipartisan cosponsorship give it a plausible path if it ever gets one.
